prompt: Write the introduction section of an academic paper titled “Do Submillimeter Galaxies Trace Megaparsec Large-scale Structures? An Overdensity Analysis of 449 Submillimeter Galaxies in COSMOS”. The paper is in astrophysics. About 700 words. Output only the text of the introduction, with no heading.
raw:
Submillimeter galaxies (SMGs) represent the most extreme population of dust-obscured, star-forming galaxies in the early universe. First discovered in deep single-dish submillimeter surveys over two decades ago, these systems exhibit prodigious star formation rates ranging from hundreds to thousands of solar masses per year, powered by vast reservoirs of molecular gas and shrouded in dense clouds of interstellar dust (e.g., Blain et al. 2002; Casey et al. 2014). Reaching their peak number density at redshifts $z \sim 2$–$3$, SMGs contribute significantly to the cosmic star formation rate density during the epoch of peak galaxy assembly. Due to their high stellar masses, compact morphologies, and rapid gas depletion timescales, SMGs are widely considered to be the high-redshift progenitors of the most massive quiescent elliptical galaxies observed in the local universe, including the brightest cluster galaxies residing at the centers of modern galaxy clusters.

In the standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmological paradigm, the formation and evolution of massive galaxies are intimately linked to the growth of large-scale structures (LSS). The most massive dark matter halos collapse early in the highest-density peaks of the primordial matter distribution, which subsequently evolve into the nodes and filaments of the cosmic web on megaparsec (Mpc) scales. Consequently, if SMGs indeed inhabit the most massive dark matter halos at high redshift, they are theoretically expected to be strongly clustered and to trace significant overdensities of galaxies, such as forming galaxy protoclusters. Furthermore, dense megaparsec-scale environments provide the ideal physical conditions—namely, elevated galaxy merger rates and enhanced cold gas accretion along cosmic filaments—to trigger the intense, short-lived starbursts characteristic of the SMG phase.

Despite these compelling theoretical expectations, observational efforts to determine whether SMGs reliably trace Mpc-scale structures have yielded conflicting results. Early angular and spatial clustering analyses of single-dish-selected SMGs suggested that they reside in massive dark matter halos ($M_{\mathrm{h}} \sim 10^{12.5}$–$10^{13}\,M_{\odot}$; e.g., Hickox et al. 2012; Wilkinson et al. 2017), and numerous individual protoclusters have been identified via overdensities of submillimeter sources (e.g., Chapman et al. 2009; Casey et al. 2015). Conversely, several direct environmental studies have found that many SMGs inhabit average, field-like densities, challenging the notion that they are universal signposts of protoclusters (e.g., Miller et al. 2015; Danielson et al. 2017). These discrepancies are largely driven by observational systematics: single-dish telescopes suffer from coarse angular resolution, leading to source blending that can artificially boost clustering signals and complicate counterpart identification. Moreover, small sample sizes, cosmic variance, and large redshift uncertainties have historically prevented statistically robust measurements of the Mpc-scale environments surrounding SMGs.

Overcoming these limitations requires both high-resolution interferometric submillimeter observations and wide-field, deep multi-wavelength ancillary data. Interferometers such as the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) resolve single-dish blends and pinpoint SMG positions to sub-arcsecond accuracy, enabling unambiguous counterpart identification in optical and near-infrared imaging. When combined with the Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS; Scoville et al. 2007), which spans $2\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ with deep, homogeneous photometry from the ultraviolet to the radio, it becomes possible to map the underlying galaxy density field with high precision. The wide area of COSMOS mitigates cosmic variance and captures structures on scales of tens of comoving megaparsecs, while its extensive catalog of accurate photometric and spectroscopic redshifts allows for the construction of well-matched control samples to isolate the true environmental preferences of SMGs.

In this paper, we present a comprehensive overdensity analysis of 449 SMGs in the COSMOS field to test whether SMGs trace megaparsec-scale large-scale structures. Utilizing the deep COSMOS multi-wavelength galaxy catalog, we measure the local galaxy overdensity around each SMG on scales of $1$ to $10\,\mathrm{cMpc}$ across $1 \lesssim z \lesssim 4$. By comparing the environments of our SMG sample against stellar-mass- and redshift-matched control samples of normal star-forming and quiescent galaxies, we evaluate whether SMGs preferentially reside in overdense regions and investigate how their environments depend on redshift and submillimeter flux density. This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the SMG sample and COSMOS datasets. Section 3 details our density field and control sample methodology. We present our results in Section 4, discuss their implications for galaxy evolution and protocluster identification in Section 5, and summarize our conclusions in Section 6. Throughout this work, we adopt a flat $\Lambda$CDM cosmology with $H_0 = 70\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} = 0.3$, and $\Omega_{\Lambda} = 0.7$.
